analysis.one_liner: Sets the federal minimum wage at a living wage, roughly $15.64 an hour, recalculated every four years.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to a living wage — about $15.64 an hour — was never taken up by the House committee it was sent to and died with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the federal minimum wage from a number set by Congress ($7.25) to a formula: enough that a person working full-time, year-round earns 25.5% more than the poverty line for a family of four — about $15.64 an hour today. The Labor Department would recalculate it every four years and could never lower it. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 1 million or more workers paid the federal minimum of $7.25, plus many earning slightly above it, would see their pay rise substantially — to roughly double for a full-time minimum-wage worker, lifting a year of full-time work above the poverty line for a family of four [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets the federal minimum wage at the hourly rate a full-time worker needs to earn an annual income 25.5% above the federal poverty threshold for a family of four — about $15.64 under current thresholds, more than double the $7.25 minimum.
Requires the Department of Labor to recompute the wage every four years and bars it from ever setting a lower rate, so the floor could not erode with inflation.
Explicitly allows states, cities, and tribes to set higher minimum wages of their own.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum or near-minimum wages — concentrated in restaurants, retail, hospitality, and care work — would bear the added payroll cost, some of which could be passed to consumers through higher prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The wage would jump from $7.25 to roughly $15.64 with no multi-year phase-in, the steepest single increase in federal minimum wage history, which opponents argued could strain small businesses and raise prices.
The formula sets one national wage for the 48 contiguous states based on a four-person-family poverty threshold, so the same rate applies in low- and high-cost regions alike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to low-wage workers would be substantial and direct: a raise to roughly $15.64 would lift the annual earnings of a full-time minimum-wage worker well above the poverty threshold and would most benefit workers in the many states whose minimums sit at or near $7.25 [S2][S3]. The main cost is borne by employers of low-wage labor, some of which could respond with higher prices or reduced hiring, a tradeoff supporters acknowledge but did not design around — the bill contains no phase-in schedule, which would have made the sudden jump from $7.25 easier to absorb.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the congressional session ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced January 9, 2023, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its two-year lifespan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay the $7.25 federal minimum wage kept that floor in place; no worker got a raise from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the full two years of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority controlling the chamber and its committee agendas
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House and the committee agenda during the 118th Congress and did not schedule minimum wage legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or a recorded position from more than one member — it had no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan line ever formed.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (fast food, retail, hospitality, caregiving)
industries.note: These industries employ large shares of minimum-wage workers and would face directly higher payroll costs, potentially passed to consumers through prices or absorbed through scheduling and staffing changes.
Roughly doubled pay for the lowest-paid workers, moving a full-time earner's income above the family poverty threshold.
